# What is Advanced Ship Notice (ASN) in Shipping?


By[Jacqueline Nance](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/profile/jacqueline-nance-sps) , *Senior Content Marketing Manager*


Last Updated November 17, 2026


8 min read


In this article, learn about:


-


What an advance ship notice (ASN) is and what information it contains


-


How ASNs improve order visibility, inventory planning, and warehouse receiving


-


Why accurate ASNs matter for retailer compliance and eCommerce fulfillment


---


Retailers and distributors need to know where their orders stand and when they'll arrive. Real-time order updates help them make better purchasing decisions, manage budgets, and avoid keeping more inventory than necessary. With reliable information, they can spot potential delays early, keep products in stock, and meet customer expectations.


Getting that visibility requires suppliers and retailers to share important order and shipping information, often through[electronic data interchange (EDI).](https://www.spscommerce.com/what-is-edi/)


One of the most important documents in this process is the advance ship notice (ASN), which tells retailers what's being shipped and what to expect when the order arrives.


## What Is an ASN?


An ASN is an electronic document that suppliers send to retailers or distributors to provide details about an incoming shipment. It identifies what's being shipped, how much is included, how the products are packaged, and when the shipment is expected to arrive.


ASNs are commonly exchanged through the EDI 856 transaction, also called the Ship Notice/Manifest. In other systems, the document may be called a dispatch advice (DESADV) or outbound ship notice.


By sharing shipment details before delivery, suppliers give receiving teams time to prepare, helping reduce delays, improve inventory accuracy, and make warehouse operations more efficient.


### What Information Does an ASN Include?


An ASN provides answers to several important questions:


-


Which purchase orders have shipped?


-


What products and quantities are included?


-


When is the shipment expected to arrive?


-


Was the entire order shipped, or are some items missing?


-


How are the products packaged and labeled?


-


What carrier and tracking information is available?


The information included in an ASN varies depending on the retailer's requirements and the type of shipment.


For example, when a supplier ships an order to a retailer's distribution center, the ASN might show that 10 cartons containing 480 units across three[stock keeping units](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/what-is-a-stock-keeping-unit-sku) (SKUs) are on their way, with delivery expected Thursday morning.


Knowing what's arriving and when helps the retailer's receiving team plan ahead, schedule dock space, and make sure enough employees are available to unload the shipment.


**Related Reading:** **[EDI 856 Advance Shipping Notice (ASN)](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/edi-856-ship-notice-manifest)


## How Does an Advance Ship Notice Work?


The ASN connects shipping activity with the retailer's receiving process. Once a supplier prepares an order for shipment, the shipping details are collected and sent electronically to the buyer.


The process typically follows four steps.


### 1. The Supplier Prepares the Shipment


The supplier picks, packs, and labels the products according to the retailer's requirements. Depending on those requirements, cartons and pallets may receive unique barcode labels that identify their contents.


### 2. The Supplier Sends the ASN


The supplier transmits the ASN, often using EDI 856, with details such as purchase order numbers, item quantities, packaging information, and shipment identification numbers.


The ASN must be sent within the timeframe required by the receiving retailer or distributor.


### 3. The Retailer Prepares for Delivery


The retailer's warehouse or distribution center uses the ASN to anticipate incoming inventory, schedule receiving activities, and identify potential differences between the original purchase order and the shipped quantities.


### 4. The Receiving Team Verifies the Shipment


When the shipment arrives, warehouse employees can scan carton or pallet barcodes and compare the results with the ASN.


If the shipment matches the notice, the receiving process can move forward quickly. Missing cartons, unexpected quantities, or labeling errors can be identified and investigated.


This process helps retailers reduce manual data entry and gives suppliers a more reliable way to communicate what they've shipped.


## What Are the Benefits of Advance Ship Notices?


Accurate ASNs help retailers and distributors manage incoming shipments more efficiently. They also help suppliers reduce shipping discrepancies and meet trading partner requirements.


### Improve Order and Shipment Visibility


An ASN gives buyers an earlier view of incoming inventory. Instead of waiting until products arrive to confirm shipment details, retailers can see what has shipped and prepare accordingly.


This visibility helps receiving teams schedule dock appointments, assign warehouse labor, and plan how products will move through the facility.


It can also support cross-docking, where products move directly from an inbound shipment to an outbound shipment without being placed into long-term storage.


For example, a grocery distribution center receives an ASN showing that a pallet contains products destined for three different stores. Because the ASN identifies the shipment's contents, the distribution center can plan how to sort and move those products to outbound trucks.


### Support More Accurate Inventory Planning


ASNs help retailers understand how much inventory is on its way and whether the quantities shipped match the original purchase order. With this information, buyers can make better purchasing decisions, anticipate potential shortages, and manage their open-to-buy budgets.


For example, if a retailer orders 1,000 units but the ASN shows that only 800 were shipped, the buying team can identify the shortfall before delivery. They may be able to adjust replenishment plans or arrange additional inventory to avoid running out of stock.


Although an ASN does not confirm that goods have been received, it provides valuable information about inbound inventory that can support planning until the shipment is physically verified.


### Speed Up Warehouse Receiving With Barcode Scanning


One of the biggest operational advantages of an ASN is its ability to support barcode-based receiving. When suppliers include carton or pallet identification numbers in the ASN, warehouse employees can scan the corresponding labels as shipments arrive. This reduces the need to manually count and enter every product during receiving, provided the shipment and ASN data match.


For example, a supplier labels 10 cartons with unique barcodes and includes those identifiers in the ASN. At the receiving dock, an employee scans each carton as it's unloaded. If all 10 cartons match the ASN, the warehouse can verify the shipment more efficiently. If a carton is missing, the discrepancy can be flagged immediately rather than discovered days later.


**Related Reading:**[What Is EDI?](https://www.spscommerce.com/what-is-edi/)


### Improve eCommerce and Drop-Shipping Visibility


ASNs also play an important role in eCommerce fulfillment, particularly when suppliers ship products directly to consumers.


In a[drop-shipping](https://www.spscommerce.com/) arrangement, the supplier fulfills an order on behalf of the retailer. The ASN can provide shipment confirmation, carrier information, and tracking numbers from services such as FedEx, UPS, or USPS.


The retailer can then share tracking details with the customer, helping shoppers follow their orders from shipment through delivery.


This visibility becomes especially important during peak shopping periods, when order volumes increase and customers expect accurate delivery updates.


Reliable shipment information helps retailers answer customer questions, identify potential delays, and manage expectations when delivery timelines change.


### Reduce Shipping Errors and Retailer Compliance Issues


Many retailers require suppliers to send ASNs in a specific format and within a defined timeframe. They may also require shipment details to match carton labels, purchase orders, and the products physically delivered.


When ASN information is missing, late, or inaccurate, receiving teams may need to spend additional time investigating discrepancies.


Depending on the retailer's compliance program, these errors can also result in chargebacks or other penalties.


Suppliers can reduce these risks by validating ASN data before transmission, following retailer-specific labeling requirements, and confirming that shipment quantities match the information sent to the buyer.


## Frequently Asked Questions About Advance Ship Notices


### Is an ASN the Same as an EDI 856?


An ASN is the shipping notice itself, while EDI 856 is the electronic transaction format commonly used to send it. The terms are often used interchangeably in retail supply chains. Other standards, such as EDIFACT DESADV, can communicate similar shipment information, and some trading partners exchange ASN data through APIs.


### Who Sends an ASN, and Who Receives It?


The supplier, manufacturer, or vendor typically sends the ASN to the retailer, distributor, or other receiving organization. For drop-ship orders, the retailer may receive the ASN from the supplier and use its tracking information to update the customer's order status. The exact process depends on the trading partners involved.


### When Should an ASN Be Sent?


An ASN should be sent according to the receiving trading partner's requirements, generally after shipment details are finalized and before the goods arrive. Some retailers establish specific deadlines tied to shipment departure or delivery. Suppliers should review each retailer's guidelines because late or inaccurate ASNs may result in compliance penalties.


### What Is an SSCC-18 Number?


An SSCC-18, or Serial Shipping Container Code, is an 18-digit identifier used to identify an individual logistics unit, such as a carton or pallet. It is typically encoded in a GS1-128 barcode on a shipping label. When the identifier is included in the ASN, receiving teams can scan the label and match it to the shipment information.


## Why Are Accurate ASNs Important for Supply Chain Efficiency?


Accurate advance ship notices help to understand what's coming before it reaches the receiving docks. That visibility supports better inventory planning, more efficient warehouse operations, and faster identification of shipment discrepancies.


When ASN data matches the physical shipment and meets retailer requirements, receiving teams can process deliveries with fewer exceptions. For eCommerce and drop-ship orders, the same shipment information can help retailers keep customers informed about their deliveries.


As retail operations become more complex, consistent and accurate shipment communication becomes increasingly important. Because ASN timing, labeling, and formatting requirements vary by retailer, suppliers need processes that keep shipment data accurate across their trading partners.


To learn more about the information included in an ASN and how it is exchanged, explore the[EDI 856 Advance Shipping Notice guide](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/edi-856-ship-notice-manifest) .
